# Distributed Deployment: Cloud, Fog, Edge {#sec-distributed-deployment}

::: {.callout-note title="Status: deep rewrite 2026-05 — code-verified against `origin/main`"}
This chapter has been rewritten end-to-end against the actual
distributed source on `origin/main`. An earlier version
(2026-05-08) treated distribution as research roadmap on the
basis of 2024 design documents. That treatment was wrong; the
distributed layer was already shipping. This rewrite is built
from a careful read of `nes-distributed/`, `nes-network/`, and
the `Placement/` subtree of `nes-query-optimizer/`.
:::

NebulaStream's vision in Chapter 1 promised cloud-edge-sensor
deployments. Earlier readers of this book might have been
forgiven for assuming, from the chapter status callouts, that
such deployments were research roadmap. They are not. As of
`origin/main` the engine has a working distributed layer:
operators are placed across workers by a mixed-integer linear
program, network channels carry tuples between them over a
Rust-implemented data plane, and the coordinator aggregates
distributed query status with a clean precedence rule for
failure modes.

This chapter walks through the implementation. It is one of the
two longest chapters in the book — alongside Chapter 15 — because
distribution is structurally the largest single piece of the
engine's recent evolution.

---

## 19.1 The five new types {#sec-distributed-types}

Five types in `nes-distributed/include/` carry the distributed
abstractions. The signatures matter because every other
distributed component plugs into them.

**`DistributedLogicalPlan`** is the post-placement plan. It maps
each worker to the local logical plans that will run on that
worker, and keeps the original global plan for reference:

```cpp
// nes-distributed/include/DistributedLogicalPlan.hpp (sketch)
class DistributedLogicalPlan {
    std::unordered_map<Host, std::vector<LogicalPlan>> localPlansByHost;
    LogicalPlan globalPlan;
    DistributedQueryId id;
public:
    const std::vector<LogicalPlan>& operator[](const Host& host) const;  // throws out_of_range
    const LogicalPlan& getGlobalPlan() const;
    DistributedQueryId getId() const;
};
```

A worker's view of the world is the slice it gets through the
`operator[]` lookup — typically a single local `LogicalPlan` per
worker, but a worker can host several logical plans of the same
distributed query if the placer fragmented the global plan that
way.

**`DistributedQuery`** is the runtime counterpart: it tracks
which local query IDs are running on which workers.

```cpp
// nes-distributed/include/DistributedQuery.hpp (sketch)
class DistributedQuery {
    std::unordered_map<Host, std::vector<QueryId>> queriesByHost;
public:
    auto iterate() const;  // flattens to (Host, QueryId) tuples
};
```

The flattening helper `iterate()` is what the coordinator's
polling loop uses: one pass through every (worker, local-query)
pair, collecting status from each.

**`NetworkTopology`** is the graph of workers. The implementation
in `nes-distributed/include/NetworkTopology.hpp` is a directed
acyclic graph with explicit upstream and downstream edges, plus
DFS path-finding:

```cpp
// nes-distributed/include/NetworkTopology.hpp (sketch)
class NetworkTopology {
    void addNode(NodeId id, std::vector<NodeId> downstreamNodes);
    void removeNode(NodeId id);
    std::vector<std::vector<NodeId>> findPaths(NodeId src, NodeId dest,
                                                Direction dir) const;
};
```

`addNode` performs cycle detection and throws `InvalidTopology`
(exception code 2301; see @sec-distributed-exceptions) if adding
a node would create a cycle. The DAG constraint matters because
the placer's connectivity check assumes acyclicity.

**`WorkerCatalog`** holds the registry of workers and owns the
topology:

```cpp
// nes-distributed/include/WorkerCatalog.hpp (sketch)
class WorkerCatalog {
    std::unordered_map<Host, WorkerConfig> workersByHost;
    NetworkTopology topology;
    uint64_t version;
public:
    void addWorker(Host host, WorkerConfig config);
    const WorkerConfig& getWorker(const Host& host) const;
    NetworkTopology getTopology() const;  // returns a snapshot
};
```

The version counter is how clients detect catalog changes
(workers joining or leaving) without consulting the catalog
itself for every operation.

**`WorkerConfig`** is per-worker configuration. Its most
distinctive feature is **dual addressing**:

```cpp
// nes-distributed/include/WorkerConfig.hpp (sketch)
struct WorkerConfig {
    Host management;    // gRPC management endpoint (port 8080)
    Host dataAddress;   // Data-plane endpoint (network channels)
    std::variant<CapacityKind::Unlimited, CapacityKind::Limited> capacity;
    std::vector<Host> downstream;
    SingleNodeWorkerConfiguration workerConfig;
};
```

Workers have *two* addresses. The coordinator uses
`management` for gRPC control-plane traffic — registering a
query, polling status, asking for shutdown. Worker-to-worker
data flow uses `dataAddress`. Forgetting which is which is one
of the most common bugs the placer guards against; we will see
why in @sec-decomposition.

::: {.callout-note title="Example 19.1: a five-worker topology"}
A small fog-style deployment:

```
   cloud (192.168.1.10)
   ↑      ↑
   │      │
gw-east  gw-west       (gateways)
 ↑   ↑    ↑   ↑
 │   │    │   │
 sensor-1 sensor-2 sensor-3 sensor-4
```

The catalog has five workers. The topology has nine edges. A
query reading from sensor-1, filtering, and sinking to cloud
has multiple valid placements: the filter can run on sensor-1,
on gw-east, or on cloud. The placer picks one. The next section
shows how.
:::

---

## 19.2 Operator placement: an integer linear program {#sec-placement-ilp}

Placing operators across workers is the central decision in
distributed query execution. Get it right and you minimise
network traffic, exploit locality, respect hardware affinities.
Get it wrong and a join over a hundred-megabyte stream gets
shipped across a slow WAN link unnecessarily.

NebulaStream's placer is in
`nes-query-optimizer/include/Placement/BottomUpPlacement.hpp`
and its implementation. The class name is misleading: despite
"BottomUp", the algorithm is not greedy bottom-up traversal. It
is an **integer linear program** solved by **HiGHS**
[@highs-solver], a state-of-the-art open-source MIP solver.

The ILP formulation:

- **Variables.** One binary variable per (operator, node) pair.
  A query with twelve operators and a five-node topology has
  sixty variables.
- **Constraints.**
  1. Each operator is assigned to exactly one node.
  2. Per-node capacity is respected. The demand of each
     operator is 1 for compute operators (filter, join,
     aggregate) and 0 for sources and sinks. Capacity is
     either `Unlimited` or a positive integer.
  3. Sources and sinks are *fixed* to their declared host;
     the placer cannot move them.
  4. Connectivity: for every parent-child operator pair, the
     placement must admit a topology path between the parent's
     node and the child's node.
- **Objective.** Minimise the total *hop distance* from each
  operator to its source descendants. Operators "want" to be
  close to data.
- **Solver settings.** 5-second timeout; accept solutions
  within 1% of optimal.

The variable-creation pass is short and direct:

```cpp
// nes-query-optimizer/src/Placement/BottomUpPlacement.cpp (sketch)
for (const LogicalOperator& op : BFSRange(plan.getRootOperators().front())) {
    for (const auto& [node, _] : topology) {
        auto index = static_cast<int>(model.reverseIndex.size());
        model.operatorPlacementMatrix[{op.getId(), node}] = index;
        checkError(Highs_addCol(model.highs, index, 0, 1, 0, nullptr, nullptr),
                   model.highs);
        checkError(Highs_changeColIntegrality(model.highs, index,
                                              kHighsVarTypeInteger),
                   model.highs);
        model.reverseIndex.emplace_back(op.getId(), node);
    }
}
```

The result, after solving, is a map from `OperatorId` to `Host`.
The placer attaches a `PlacementTrait` to each operator with
that host:

```cpp
// nes-query-optimizer/include/Traits/PlacementTrait.hpp (sketch)
class PlacementTrait : public Trait {
    Host onNode;
public:
    explicit PlacementTrait(Host onNode);
    Host getNode() const;
};
```

Like every trait in NebulaStream's logical algebra (Chapter 6),
`PlacementTrait` is immutable; the operator carries it through
every subsequent phase.

::: {.callout-note title="Example 19.2: the sixty-variable problem"}
For our Example 19.1 topology and a query

```
SELECT temp FROM sensor-1 WHERE temp > 100 INTO cloud-sink
```

(four operators: source, selection, projection, sink), the ILP
has 4 × 5 = 20 binary variables, 4 "exactly-one-node"
constraints, 5 capacity constraints, 2 fixed-placement
constraints (source → sensor-1, sink → cloud), and 3 connectivity
constraints (one per operator-pair edge). The objective is the
sum of hop distances from each operator to sensor-1.

The optimal placement: source on sensor-1, selection on
sensor-1 (zero hops, exploits locality), projection on
gateway-east (one hop, then aggregating before the long climb
to cloud), sink on cloud. Total objective: small. The query
filters at the edge before crossing the slow link to the
cloud, which is exactly what "in-network processing" in the
README's vision means.
:::

## 19.3 From placed plan to network channels {#sec-decomposition}

A logical plan with `PlacementTrait`s is not yet executable. The
`QueryDecomposer`
(`nes-query-optimizer/include/Placement/QueryDecomposition.hpp`)
walks the placed plan, groups operators by node, and *inserts
network channels* wherever a parent-child edge crosses a node
boundary.

The substitution is local. A logical edge `OpA → OpB` where
`OpA.placement == nodeX` and `OpB.placement == nodeY` becomes:

```
nodeX:  OpA → NetworkSink(channelId, bind=X.dataAddress, dest=Y.dataAddress)
nodeY:  NetworkSource(channelId, bind=Y.dataAddress) → OpB
```

The two new operators share a fresh `ChannelId` (a UUID) so the
runtime can correlate sender and receiver. Both consult the
worker catalog's `WorkerConfig` to find the *data-plane*
addresses (not the gRPC management address — the dual-addressing
distinction from @sec-distributed-types matters here).

The result of decomposition is a `DistributedLogicalPlan`: one
local plan per worker, each starting at a source or
NetworkSource and ending at a sink or NetworkSink. From here
each local plan goes through the ordinary single-node compile
pipeline (Chapter 9-12), producing a per-worker
`CompiledQueryPlan`. The coordinator ships each compiled plan
to its worker over gRPC.

::: {.callout-tip title="Real-system reference: how Flink does this"}
Apache Flink's analogous step is its `JobGraph` → `ExecutionGraph`
transition. Flink also inserts shuffle/forward edges that map to
network exchanges. The differences:

1. Flink's placer is heuristic; NebulaStream's is exact (ILP).
2. Flink models per-operator parallelism explicitly (an
   operator may run on N parallel instances). NebulaStream's
   placer produces one operator instance per node by default;
   intra-node parallelism is handled at the runtime level
   (Chapter 15).

The exact-vs-heuristic trade-off is interesting. Flink scales
to thousands of operators per query partly because it does not
solve a global optimisation problem at placement time.
NebulaStream's HiGHS solver is fast on small queries, but its
5-second timeout is a hint that the team has not yet stressed
it against very large topologies.
:::

## 19.4 The data plane: Rust channels and an in-memory fast path {#sec-data-plane}

Tuples cross workers via the `nes-network/` module. The data
plane is implemented in Rust and exposed to C++ through FFI
bindings. There are two channel implementations:

**`TcpCommunication`** for genuine inter-worker traffic. Tokio
sockets, configurable I/O thread count, conventional TCP
flow control.

**`MemCom`** for workers co-located in the same process — useful
for tests and for a future deployment mode that pins multiple
workers to one machine. MemCom uses tokio's in-memory
`SimplexStream` with 1 MiB buffers and zero serialisation:

```rust
// nes-network/network/src/memcom.rs (sketch)
pub struct MemCom {
    listeners: RwLock<HashMap<ConnectionIdentifier, Sender<Channel>>>,
}

impl MemCom {
    pub fn bind(&self, id: ConnectionIdentifier) -> Receiver<Channel> {
        let (tx, rx) = channel();
        self.listeners.write().unwrap().insert(id, tx);
        rx
    }

    pub fn connect(&self, id: ConnectionIdentifier) -> Result<Channel> {
        // Retry with exponential backoff: 2ms, 4ms, ... up to 32ms,
        // 10 retries total before giving up.
        for delay_ms in [2u64, 4, 8, 16, 32, 32, 32, 32, 32, 32] {
            if let Some(tx) = self.listeners.read().unwrap().get(&id).cloned() {
                let (a_to_b, b_to_a) = simplex_pair();
                tx.send(b_to_a)?;
                return Ok(a_to_b);
            }
            std::thread::sleep(Duration::from_millis(delay_ms));
        }
        Err(NotConnected)
    }
}
```

The `SimplexStream` is half-duplex; a bidirectional channel is
two simplex streams glued together. The Rust side uses
`#[pinned_drop]` to ensure that abandoning one half closes the
other — without this, blocked readers on the other end of an
abandoned writer would hang indefinitely.

**Backpressure** is configured per channel via the
`WorkerNetworkConfiguration`:

```cpp
// nes-network/interface/WorkerNetworkConfiguration.hpp (sketch)
struct WorkerNetworkConfiguration {
    uint64_t senderQueueSize = 1024;     // buffers awaiting send
    uint64_t maxPendingAcks = 64;        // in-flight unacked
    uint64_t receiverQueueSize = 10;     // receiver-side buffer
    uint64_t backpressureUpperThreshold;
    uint64_t backpressureLowerThreshold;
    uint64_t senderIOThreads = 1;        // 0 = use core count
    uint64_t receiverIOThreads = 1;
};
```

The defaults are conservative; production deployments will
typically tune them per-channel based on observed throughput.

::: {.callout-note title="Example 19.3: a tuple's cross-worker journey"}
A 8-KiB `TupleBuffer` produced on worker A and consumed on
worker B:

1. Operator emits buffer; the `NetworkSink` enqueues it onto
   the channel's `senderQueue` (max 1024 buffers).
2. The Rust `Channel::send` half writes the buffer's bytes
   onto the TCP socket (or the in-memory simplex stream for
   MemCom).
3. On worker B, the Rust receiver reads the bytes into a
   reconstructed `TupleBuffer` allocated from worker B's local
   buffer pool.
4. The `NetworkSource` returns the buffer; the next
   operator's `execute` is called.

Watermarks (Chapter 7) ride along in the buffer's metadata:
the receiving side's `MultiOriginWatermarkProcessor` consumes
the same `OriginId`/`SequenceNumber`/`Watermark` triple that
the sending side emitted, and the engine's notion of progress
is consistent across the boundary.
:::

## 19.5 The coordinator and the status hierarchy {#sec-coordinator-status}

Above the workers sits the **coordinator**, which is being
integrated on the `ys-coordinator-integration` branch and uses a
Rust implementation with a C++/FFI bridge. Within `main`, the
relevant runtime data structure is `DistributedQuery`, plus its
status snapshot machinery.

A distributed query's "current status" is a function of every
worker's local query status. NebulaStream defines six states:

| State | Meaning |
|---|---|
| Registered | All workers have accepted the query but none have started |
| Running | At least one worker is executing |
| PartiallyStopped | Some workers have stopped; others still running |
| Stopped | All workers report stopped |
| Failed | At least one worker has reported a hard failure |
| Unreachable | At least one worker is unreachable (gRPC error) |

The aggregation is in
`nes-distributed/src/DistributedQuery.cpp` and follows a strict
precedence order:

```cpp
// nes-distributed/src/DistributedQuery.cpp (sketch)
DistributedQueryStatus DistributedQueryStatusSnapshot::getGlobalQueryStatus() const {
    if (any({QueryStatus::Failed})) {
        return DistributedQueryStatus::Failed;
    }
    if (hasConnectionException) {
        return DistributedQueryStatus::Unreachable;
    }
    if (all({QueryStatus::Stopped})) {
        return DistributedQueryStatus::Stopped;
    }
    // ... Running / PartiallyStopped / Registered ...
}
```

`Failed` dominates `Unreachable`: a hard failure on a reachable
worker is more authoritative than the silence of an unreachable
one. `Unreachable` dominates `Stopped`: if any worker is
silent, we cannot claim the whole query is stopped. This is
exactly the precedence you want for an operator triaging a
broken deployment.

Per-query metrics (start time, last activity, stop time) are
coalesced across workers: start = `min` (the earliest worker to
start), running = `max` (the latest activity), stop = `max`
(the last worker to stop).

## 19.6 What landed and what is still in flux {#sec-landed-vs-flux}

A reader who has gotten this far deserves a short audit of which
parts of the distribution story can be trusted today and which
are work in progress.

**Landed and stable on `origin/main`:**

- `DistributedLogicalPlan`, `DistributedQuery`, `NetworkTopology`,
  `WorkerCatalog`, `WorkerConfig`.
- HiGHS-based ILP placement.
- Decomposition with NetworkSink/NetworkSource insertion.
- Rust TCP channel and MemCom in-memory fast path.
- Status aggregation with Failed > Unreachable > Stopped > … precedence.
- Distributed exception types (PlacementFailure 2300,
  InvalidTopology 2301, UnknownWorker 2302, DistributedFailure
  2303 — see @sec-distributed-exceptions).

**Landed but tuning is open:**

- Cost-model weights for the ILP. The hop-distance objective
  gets the right shape; calibrating it for hardware-affinity
  awareness (a GPU operator wants a GPU node) is in progress.
- Backpressure thresholds. The defaults are reasonable; per-
  workload tuning is pending.

**Still in flight:**

- The Rust coordinator integration on the
  `ys-coordinator-integration` branch.
- Failure recovery (a worker crash today fails the query;
  Chapter 22 discusses this open problem).
- Adaptive re-placement when topology changes mid-query.

Where the earlier chapters of this book make claims about
distributed behaviour, those claims are anchored on this
chapter's verified content. Chapter 7's discussion of
watermark propagation is the principal cross-reference: the
four-tuple progress identifiers we met there are exactly what
the receiving side of a `NetworkSource` consumes, and the
`MultiOriginWatermarkProcessor` is what synthesises them into a
unified progress view across origins from different workers.

## 19.7 The exception taxonomy for distribution {#sec-distributed-exceptions}

The distributed layer has a dedicated 23XX block in
`nes-common/include/ExceptionDefinitions.inc`:

| Code | Name | Trigger |
|---|---|---|
| 2300 | `PlacementFailure` | ILP solver returned no feasible solution |
| 2301 | `InvalidTopology` | adding the proposed edge would create a cycle |
| 2302 | `UnknownWorker` | catalog lookup for a host that was never registered |
| 2303 | `DistributedFailure` | catch-all for worker-side errors that propagate to the coordinator |

The 5XXX network range (which Chapter 17 catalogues fully) does
NOT have separate distributed-specific entries; network
disruptions are reported as the same connection errors a
single-node gRPC client would see, with the
`hasConnectionException` flag in
`DistributedQueryStatusSnapshot` carrying the distributed
semantics.

---

## Summary {#sec-ch19-summary}

NebulaStream's distributed layer rests on five abstractions
(`DistributedLogicalPlan`, `DistributedQuery`, `NetworkTopology`,
`WorkerCatalog`, `WorkerConfig`), an ILP-based placer (HiGHS
solver, hop-distance objective, 5-second timeout), a
decomposition pass that inserts network channels at placement
boundaries, and a Rust-implemented data plane offering both TCP
and in-memory MemCom transports. Worker status is aggregated
across the cluster with a precedence order that puts Failed
above Unreachable above Stopped. The four distributed exception
codes (2300-2303) are a thin layer over the engine's general
error model. What remains in flight: cost-model calibration,
the coordinator integration, failure recovery, adaptive
re-placement.

---

## Reading exercises {#sec-ch19-exercises}

::: {.callout-important title="Reading exercise 19.1: read the ILP construction"}
Open `nes-query-optimizer/src/Placement/BottomUpPlacement.cpp`
on `origin/main`. Identify:

1. The variable construction loop (one binary var per
   operator-node pair).
2. The capacity constraint.
3. The connectivity constraint.
4. The objective function.

Sketch on paper the ILP that would be produced for the query
and topology in Example 19.2. How many variables, how many
constraints?
:::

::: {.callout-important title="Reading exercise 19.2: trace MemCom"}
Read `nes-network/network/src/memcom.rs`. The connect path
retries with exponential backoff. What is the maximum total
backoff before giving up? Why does the bind path use a Tokio
`channel::Sender<Channel>` rather than a vector?
:::

::: {.callout-important title="Reading exercise 19.3: status precedence"}
Construct (on paper) every combination of three workers
reporting status. For each combination, predict
`getGlobalQueryStatus()`'s output. Verify against
`nes-distributed/src/DistributedQuery.cpp`. The precedence
ordering should be unambiguous; if you find an ambiguous case,
that is a bug worth reporting.
:::

::: {.callout-important title="Reading exercise 19.4: a fault-injection thought experiment"}
Pick a worker in your hypothetical 5-worker topology. Imagine
it crashes mid-query. Walk through what the engine actually
does today: the coordinator's poll fails, the
`hasConnectionException` flag flips, the global status becomes
`Unreachable`. What does *not* happen automatically: state
recovery, re-placement, query restart. Map each "does not
happen" item to the open-problem item in @sec-distributed-future.
:::
